summary:
Kastamonu province stands under the national framework of Turkey: the criminal law, health regulation, identity-document rules and detention practice that determine what a trans visitor faces are set at national level and apply in Kastamonu as elsewhere. No statute, enforcement action, incident or court decision specific to Kastamonu appears in the sources assembled for this record.

On 29 October 2025 Human Rights Watch reported a leaked omnibus draft, the 11th Judicial Package, that would amend the penal code to imprison conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality for up to three years, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies for up to four years. The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25, with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and trans people receiving care deemed illegal up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and Human Rights Watch warns it would force treatment underground and expose people to arrest and pretrial detention.

The draft had not been enacted when reported, and its pending status has not stopped authorities from applying equivalent prohibitions. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release; legal experts cited in that reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women held said police issued no fines but documented her anyway, and noted the new law had not been passed even as it was being applied to them.

Document rules turn every such stop into an outing risk. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. A trans visitor stopped at a checkpoint must produce documents that can be compared directly against presentation.

Kaos GL's 2025 review records roughly 313 violations overall, about two and a half times the previous year, alongside 299 detention decisions. It counts six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings, with transgender people the group most affected, and 89 torture and ill-treatment violations, up from 51 the prior year. Violence and the state response to it remain asymmetric: in August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker, who was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest.

Trans prisoners are placed by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported four transgender inmates sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before, a prolonged delay before medical staff arrived, prosecutors entering two days later, and no witness statements taken. The case was raised in parliament on 12 December 2025 and confirmed that a trans man had been held in a women's prison. A visitor held overnight faces the same placement logic and the same documented conditions: arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required electronic reports to be issued, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to care.
tangentialFactors:
Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia. Public assembly around Pride events is a standing flashpoint, and Kastamonu's sources record no comparable local gathering of that scale.

The Erdoğan government frames its position as protecting "the family" and "public morals", language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people. Kaos GL records that this framing produced "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions during 2025, an environment in which street-level stops and documentation of trans people proceeded without a statute in force.

Reported enforcement concentrates on Istanbul, where the stops, the Pride monitoring and the Yaşam case all occurred. Kastamonu is a smaller provincial centre without that metropolitan policing density, but the documentary and ID obligations are national, so the absence of Kastamonu-specific reporting reflects the absence of monitoring rather than an established difference in practice.

Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people. It predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is historical evidence of the depth of the regime, not a statement of current law.
localsOnly:
Kaos GL's 2025 review finds hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy. "Year of the Family" instructions were issued to public institutions, an LGBTI+ association was closed for the first time in years with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members, and artistic events were cancelled or banned. The same review counts freedom-of-expression violations rising from 216 to 540 across the year.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Turkey, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence.

The death of the transgender prisoner Poyraz at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025 drew demands for an independent investigation coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın. Opposition MP Sevda Karaca raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025, confirming that Turkey places trans prisoners according to their registered sex and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Transition-related care operates under a Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, which followed a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular adding "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports. Hospitals are barred from recording the "other" option and must issue electronic reports, a change that profiles trans patients in official records; online framing of the change was contested as an "LGBT opening".

Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the leaked 11th Judicial Package on the terms reported by Human Rights Watch, including the raise in the minimum age for gender-affirming care to 25 and the criminal penalties on providers and recipients.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory contains a Kastamonu-specific statute, enforcement action, incident, health circular or court decision. All findings above are national-framework findings applied to the province, and the province's own record is unresolved rather than clear.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted is unresolved in these sources. Human Rights Watch reported it as a leaked draft on 29 October 2025 and stated it had not been passed at that point; no later status is sourced here.

Whether the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation and the Kayseri circular operate through the Kastamonu Provincial Health Directorate is not sourced. The provincial application of the electronic-reporting requirement is therefore unresolved.

Whether the "General Information Gathering" stops documented in Istanbul are carried out by police in Kastamonu is not sourced; no Kastamonu policing data was available. The national obligation to produce original identity documents at checkpoints is sourced and applies province-wide.

The formal scope of hate-crime provisions with respect to gender identity, and their enforcement in Kastamonu, are not sourced. Kaos GL's counts of hate-motivated killings are national totals with no provincial breakdown, as is the Kaos GL figure of 299 detention decisions.
